title: Kitchen Orders
summary: Fix a restaurant's ticket clock, simulate dishes queuing at kitchen stations under house priority rules, then make the simulator survive game-day volumes.

overview.python:
You've joined the platform team at **Ember & Oak**, a restaurant group whose kitchens run on this kitchen display system (KDS). Tickets from the front counter and the delivery-app tablet are parsed from the printer log onto a ticket rail. Expo uses the reports to quote pickup times and to see which station is falling behind.

Every dish is cooked at one station (grill, fryer, salad or oven) by one of that station's identical cooks. Delivery-app orders get priority, and some orders carry a promised `due` time. Times are whole minutes since midnight.

Start with `README.md`, then `kitchen/tickets.py` and `kitchen/clock.py` (how the log becomes orders), `kitchen/orders.py` (the host-stand quote) and `kitchen/simulator.py` (the house rules, not implemented yet). `main.py` prints the rail and the service report for last Saturday's lunch.

phases.title: The lunch rush lands at midnight
phases.instructions:
Two reports came in after Saturday's lunch shift:

> *Expo:* "Every ticket we rang in during the noon hour shows a pickup quote around half past midnight, **the next day**. The quotes on the 11 o'clock tickets look right."

> *Floor manager:* "On the ticket rail, the 12 o'clock tickets are listed after the 1 o'clock ones, so the line keeps skipping them. The delivery promises for that hour look odd too."

Run the demo to see it for yourself. Find the root cause and fix it with a small change. The log format and the existing APIs must not change.

**Done when:** all tests in the phase 1 test file pass.
hints: Run the demo and compare a noon-hour ticket with an 11 o'clock one. Is the quote arithmetic wrong, or is the arrival minute stored on the order already wrong?

hints.python: Every stamp in the log, including `due` times, goes through `kitchen/clock.py`. Try a few by hand: `11:59am`, `12:00pm`, `12:30pm`, `1:00pm`.
hints.javascript: Every stamp in the log, including `due` times, goes through `src/clock.js`. Try a few by hand: `11:59am`, `12:00pm`, `12:30pm`, `1:00pm`.

hints.python: Look at how `parse_clock` turns the am/pm suffix into a 24-hour value. What should `12:30pm` become? And `12:30am`?
hints.javascript: Look at how `parseClock` turns the am/pm suffix into a 24-hour value. What should `12:30pm` become? And `12:30am`?

answer.python:
**Root cause.** `parse_clock` converts 12-hour stamps by adding 12 hours to every pm time:

```python
if match.group(3).lower() == "pm":
    hours += 12
```

That is right for 1pm to 11pm but wrong for the 12 o'clock hour: `12:05pm` becomes 24:05 (minute 1445, displayed as `12:05am +1`). Noon-hour tickets therefore sort after the 1pm tickets, and their quotes and due times land after midnight. The mirror-image error makes `12:05am` parse as five past noon.

**Fix.** Treat 12 as 0 before applying the suffix:

```python
hours %= 12
if match.group(3).lower() == "pm":
    hours += 12
```

**Verify.** Run the phase 1 tests; the round-trip test pushes every minute of the day through `format_clock` and back. The rail sort and the quote were never wrong: they faithfully used bad arrival minutes. A strong answer proves that by calling `parse_clock` directly instead of patching the sort.
answer.javascript:
**Root cause.** `parseClock` converts 12-hour stamps by adding 12 hours to every pm time:

```javascript
if (match[3].toLowerCase() === 'pm') hours += 12;
```

That is right for 1pm to 11pm but wrong for the 12 o'clock hour: `12:05pm` becomes 24:05 (minute 1445, displayed as `12:05am +1`). Noon-hour tickets therefore sort after the 1pm tickets, and their quotes and due times land after midnight. The mirror-image error makes `12:05am` parse as five past noon.

**Fix.** Treat 12 as 0 before applying the suffix:

```javascript
hours %= 12;
if (match[3].toLowerCase() === 'pm') hours += 12;
```

**Verify.** Run the phase 1 tests; the round-trip test pushes every minute of the day through `formatClock` and back. The rail sort and the quote were never wrong: they faithfully used bad arrival minutes. A strong answer proves that by calling `parseClock` directly instead of patching the sort.

phases.title: Simulate the line

instructions.python:
Expo wants real ready times, not host-stand guesses. Implement `simulate(orders, menu, stations)` in `kitchen/simulator.py`, following the house rules in its docstring:

- At an order's `arrival` minute, each of its dishes joins the queue of its station (`menu[dish].station`).
- A station has `cooks` identical cooks. Each makes one dish at a time, taking `menu[dish].prep` minutes. A dish started at minute `t` frees its cook at `t + prep`, and that cook may start another dish in that same minute. A dish in progress is never interrupted.
- A free cook takes the waiting dish that ranks first: `priority` (delivery-app) orders before the rest, then the earlier order `arrival`, then the lower order `id`, then the earlier position on the ticket.
- All cooks finishing and all orders arriving in a minute count **before** anyone picks a dish in that minute.
- An order is ready when its last dish finishes.

Return `KitchenRun(ready, late)`. `ready` maps every order id to its ready minute. `late` lists `(order_id, minutes_late)` for each order with a `due` time that was ready after it, sorted by order id. Finishing exactly on the due minute is on time.

The order list can be in any order. Ids are unique, every order has at least one dish, and an unknown dish raises `MenuError`. A service may run past midnight; minutes just keep counting.

**Done when:** phase 1 and phase 2 tests pass, and `python main.py` prints the full Saturday lunch report.

hints: Stations never share cooks or dishes. Picture one station at a time: a list of waiting dishes, plus the finish minutes of the dishes being cooked.

The simplest correct loop advances a clock one minute at a time: add this minute's arrivals, release cooks whose dish is done, then let each free cook take the best waiting dish. Keep that order inside the minute, or a same-minute delivery order loses out.

hints.python: Encode the rank as a tuple `(not order.priority, order.arrival, order.id, position)` so `min()` or sorting applies all four rules at once. Stop when every dish has been started, and keep each order's latest finish.
hints.javascript: Write one comparison function, `ranksAhead(a, b)`, that checks priority, then arrival, then order id, then ticket position, and use it everywhere you pick a dish. Stop when every dish has been started, and keep each order's latest finish.

answer.python:
**Approach: minute-by-minute simulation.**

1. Group orders by arrival minute. Per station keep a list of waiting dishes and a list of finish minutes for dishes on the stove.
2. From the first arrival, for each minute `t`: enqueue the dishes of orders arriving at `t`; drop finish minutes `<= t` (those cooks are free); while a cook is free and dishes wait, take the best-ranked dish, start it at `t` and record `ready[id] = max(ready[id], t + prep)`.
3. Stop once every dish has started, then build `late` from `ready` and `due`.

```python
waiting[item.station].append((not order.priority, order.arrival, order.id, position, item.prep))
...
dish = min(queue)
queue.remove(dish)
```

**Complexity.** O(T·S + D·Q) for T simulated minutes, S stations, D dishes and Q the queue length at each pick. Fine for one restaurant's service; quadratic once queues get long.

**Mistakes the tests catch:** dispatching a freed cook before admitting same-minute arrivals; LIFO or input-order queues; cooking the quickest dish on a ticket first instead of ticket order; counting a finish exactly on `due` as late; assuming the order list is sorted.

phases.title: Game day at the stadium

instructions.python:
The group's stadium kitchen wants the simulator for game-day staffing. Planners replay generated three-day festival logs against deliberately thin lines, so queues run thousands of dishes deep. The big test replays **28,000 orders (about 70,000 dishes)** and must finish in under **1 second**.

Make `simulate` fast enough for the phase 3 tests while keeping its results identical. The tests also re-check correctness on a new service, a burst of simultaneous orders and a quiet service.

Before you change code, explain where your phase 2 solution spends its time and what you'll change.

**Done when:** all phase 1–3 tests pass.

Make `simulate` fast enough for the phase 3 tests while keeping its results identical. The tests also re-check correctness on a new service, a burst of simultaneous orders and a quiet service.

hints: Measure first. How long do the station queues get during the rush, and how much work does your loop do each time a cook picks a dish? How many minutes does the clock tick through where nothing can happen?
A heap keyed by the house-rule rank hands over the next dish in O(log Q) instead of a full scan. A second heap of finish minutes tells you when the next cook frees up.

Jump the clock between events instead of ticking: with nothing waiting, jump to the next arrival; with no free cook, jump to the next finish. Release and admit everything at the new minute before dispatching. Because stations are independent, you can run this loop per station over its dishes sorted by arrival.

answer.python:
**Where phase 2 breaks.** Every pick scans the whole station queue with `min()` and `remove()`. On an overloaded line the queues hold thousands of dishes for most of the run, so 70,000 picks cost on the order of 10^8 tuple comparisons: about 5–6 s. Re-sorting each queue once per minute is better, but still pays for the whole queue on every busy minute.

**Optimized approach: a discrete-event loop with two heaps per station.**

1. Group dishes by station and sort each group by arrival.
2. `waiting` is a heap of `(not priority, arrival, order_id, position, prep)`, `stove` is a heap of finish minutes, and `free` counts idle cooks.
3. Jump the clock to the next event, release and admit everything at that minute, then dispatch:

```python
while i < n or waiting:
    if not waiting:
        clock = max(clock, dishes[i][0])   # idle: next arrival
    elif not free:
        clock = max(clock, stove[0])       # all busy: next finish
    while stove and stove[0] <= clock:
        heappop(stove); free += 1
    while i < n and dishes[i][0] <= clock:
        ...push dishes[i] onto waiting by rank...; i += 1
    while free and waiting:
        ...start heappop(waiting) at clock, push clock + prep onto stove...
```

**Complexity.** O(D log D) time and O(D) memory. The reference runs the 28,000-order test in about 0.1 s.

**Why the results are identical.** Ranks are unique (order id plus ticket position), so the heap never breaks a tie arbitrarily. Processing every finish and arrival at a minute before dispatching keeps rule 4.

**Tradeoff.** Simulating each station separately only works because stations share nothing. If a dish needed two stations, or cooks could float between stations, you would need one global event heap. A sorted list maintained with `bisect.insort` also passes in practice because memmove is fast, but each insert is O(Q).
answer.javascript:
**Where phase 2 breaks.** Every pick scans the whole station queue and `splice`s the winner out. On an overloaded line the queues hold thousands of dishes for most of the run, so 160,000 picks cost on the order of 10^9 comparisons: about 5 s even in V8. Re-sorting each queue once per minute is better, but still pays for the whole queue on every busy minute.

**Optimized approach: a discrete-event loop with two heaps per station.** JavaScript has no built-in heap, so add a small binary heap (`src/heap.js`) that takes a "comes first" predicate.

1. Group dishes by station and sort each group by arrival.
2. `waiting` is a heap ordered by `ranksAhead`, `stove` is a heap of finish minutes, and `free` counts idle cooks.
3. Jump the clock to the next event, release and admit everything at that minute, then dispatch:

```javascript
while (i < dishes.length || waiting.size) {
  if (!waiting.size) clock = Math.max(clock, dishes[i].arrival); // idle: next arrival
  else if (!free) clock = Math.max(clock, stove.peek());          // all busy: next finish
  while (stove.size && stove.peek() <= clock) { stove.pop(); free += 1; }
  while (i < dishes.length && dishes[i].arrival <= clock) waiting.push(dishes[i++]);
  while (free && waiting.size) { /* start waiting.pop() at clock, push clock + prep */ }
}
```

**Complexity.** O(D log D) time and O(D) memory. The reference runs the 64,000-order test in about 0.15 s.

**Why the results are identical.** Ranks are unique (order id plus ticket position), so the heap never breaks a tie arbitrarily. Processing every finish and arrival at a minute before dispatching keeps rule 4.

**Tradeoff.** Simulating each station separately only works because stations share nothing. If a dish needed two stations, or cooks could float between stations, you would need one global event heap. Packing the rank into a single number would make heap comparisons cheaper, at the cost of hard limits on ids and times.
